• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.
Regions
Western
•  Locust-affected countries in West and North-West Africa: 
Algeria, Chad, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, 
Senegal, Tunisia; during upsurges and plagues only: Benin, 
Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Gambia, 
Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierre 
Leone and Togo
Central
•  Locust-affected countries along the Red Sea and Gulf of 
Aden: Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Oman, Saudi Arabia, 
Somalia, Sudan, Yemen; during upsurges and plagues only: 
Bahrain, D.R. Congo, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kenya, Kuwait, 
Lebanon, Palestine, Qatar, South Sudan, Syria, Tanzania, 
Turkey, UAE and Uganda
Eastern
•  Locust-affected countries in South-West Asia: Afghanistan, 
India, Iran and Pakistan

while adult groups persisted and hopper groups continued to 
appear in Algeria’s central and northern Sahara. Some signs of 
breeding started to be reported from southern Algeria. Locust 
populations decreased in Tunisia and Morocco, though some 
groups remained. Scattered adults were present in Mauritania 
and mature groups in Niger. With the onset of summer rains, 
adult groups and small swarms are expected to move southward

southwestern Libya, western Chad, northern Niger, northern

move south into Sudan, where small-scale summer breeding 
may begin in July. In the Eastern Region, heavy monsoon 
rains reached the India–Pakistan border, potentially enabling 
very small-scale breeding, though no signiﬁ cant developments 
are expected.

WESTERN REGION
During August, summer rains continued in all Sahelian countries. 
In the ﬁ rst dekad, the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) 
was positioned south of its normal position, except in Mali, 
where it extended up to 170 km north of its usual position. 
Moderate rains were recorded in the Hodhs and Adrar regions 
of Mauritania, the Tombouctou, Timetrine and Adrar-des-Iforas 
areas of Mali, the Tamesna Plateau, Aïr Mountains and Tin-
Toumma Desert in Niger, and the Kanem, Batha, Ouaddaï, 
and Wadi Fira regions of Chad. Light to moderate rains also 
fell in southern Algeria, northern Mali, the Ténéré region of 
Niger, and Borkou area of Chad. During the second dekad, the 
ITCZ shifted northward, ranging from 50 to 100 km north of its 
normal position, from eastern Mauritania to eastern Chad, with 
an anomaly of up to 300 km further north in Algeria. Moderate 
to heavy rains were observed in Mauritania, northeastern 
Mali, southern Algeria, the Tamesna Plateau, Aïr Mountains, 
Zinder region and Tin-Toumma Desert of Niger, as well as 
from Kanem to Ennedi in Chad. Light to moderate rainfall 
were also recorded in central Algeria, northwestern Mali, and 
the Tibesti Mountains of northern Chad. In the third dekad, the 
ITCZ shifted southward, settling approximately 200 km south 
of its average position from western Mauritania to eastern Mali, 
while remaining 50 to 200 km north of its normal location from 
southern Algeria to Chad. Heavy rains continued in southern 
Mauritania, northwestern Niger, and the Borkou and Ennedi 
regions of Chad. Light to moderate rains were also reported 
in northwestern Mauritania, between Dakhla and Zouerate, 
in northern Mali, central and southern Algeria, and the Tibesti 
Mountains of Chad. Vegetation conditions improved in the 
summer breeding areas, with green vegetation observed from 
western Mauritania to Chad.
CENTRAL REGION
In August, rainfall increased in the Region. During the ﬁ rst 
dekad, the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone remained south of 
its normal position in Sudan. However, in the second and third 
dekads, it shifted up to 400 km north of its average position in 
eastern Sudan. Light to heavy rains fell during the ﬁ rst dekad 
in North Darfur, North Kordofan, Khartoum, and Kassala states 
of Sudan, as well as the western lowlands of Eritrea. In the 
second and third dekads, heavy rains continued in these areas 
and extended northward into the Northern, River Nile and Red 
Sea states, resulting in ﬂ oodings and casualties. While the 
Red Sea coast of Sudan was spared, Eritrea’s coast received 
moderate to heavy rains during the second and third dekads. 
Along the eastern Red Sea coast, light to moderate rainfall 
occurred from southern Yemen to Rabigh in Saudi Arabia 
during the ﬁ rst dekad. Rainfall intensiﬁ ed during the second 
and third dekads, with moderate to heavy rains reaching as 
far north as Yenbo in Saudi Arabia. In the interior regions of 
Yemen and Oman, light rainfall was recorded in the ﬁ rst dekad, 
increasing to moderate and heavy rainfall in the second and 
third dekads, particularly affecting the Hadramaut and Shabwah 
governorates in Yemen, the border between the two countries, 
and the Ad Dhahirah governorate in Oman. Light to moderate 
rains fell throughout the month in northwestern Somalia and Dire 
Dawa region of Ethiopia. In Egypt and northern par of Sudan, 
vegetation remained dry except in irrigated areas. Greening 
or green vegetation was observed in the southern Red Sea, 
River Nile, and Kassala states of Sudan and in the western 
lowlands of Eritrea, while the western Red Sea coast remained 
with dry vegetation. On the eastern Red Sea coast, vegetation 
was green in Jizan, greening in Qunﬁ dah, and still dry north 
of Lith in Saudi Arabia. In Oman’s interior, vegetation was dry.
EASTERN REGION
During August, heavy summer monsoon rains continued to fall 
along the Indo-Pakistan border. In the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains 
were recorded in Rajasthan in India and Cholistan in Pakistan. 
During the second dekad, moderate to heavy rainfall resumed in 
Rajasthan and Gujarat in India as well as Pakistan’s Cholistan, 
Nara, and Tharparkar Deserts. In the third dekad, moderate 
to heavy rains persisted across all summer breeding areas on 
both sides of the border. Vegetation was green in Rajasthan 
and Gujarat in India as well as Pakistan’s Cholistan, Nara, and 
Tharparkar Deserts. In Iran, vegetation was dry near Dalgan, 
while green vegetation was observed in some places between 
Shiraz and Minab, and in some sites of South Khorosan.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should connect to the Internet and 
backup the RAMSES database whenever data are added or 
changed; do not wait until the end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

scattered adults were reported, while Tunisia had very few 
isolated adults remaining. Across the Sahel, isolated adults 
were detected in Niger and Chad. Mauritania continued to 
host many scattered and isolated mature adults, and a few 
adult groups were also observed. The increased rainfall in July 
across the Sahel has created favourable breeding conditions 
for dispersed locust populations. Continued surveillance will 
be essential to monitor potential developments, and preventive 
control operations will likely be necessary. In the Central Region, 
a few adult groups were still present in Egypt. Isolated and 
scattered adults were present in Sudan, where small-scale 
summer breeding may have begun. Breeding is expected to 
continue in Sudan and may also start in Eritrea and Yemen. 
In the Eastern Region, heavy monsoon rains continued along 
the India–Pakistan border, where only a few isolated adults 
were present in Pakistan. Very small-scale breeding is likely 
to occur, though no signiﬁ cant developments are expected.

Rainfall continued in the Sahel and Sudan, and decreased 
along the Indo-Pakistan border. Green vegetation remains 
in many summer breeding areas. Rainfall has also declined 
along the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
WESTERN REGION
During September, summer rains persisted in across all Sahelian 
countries. In the ﬁ rst dekad, the Inter-Tropical Convergence 
Zone (ITCZ) extended more than 650 km north of its normal 
position in Chad and Niger, and between 50 and 200 km north 
of its usual position in Mali and Mauritania. Moderate to heavy 
rainfall was recorded in the south, center, west and north of 
Mauritania; Western Sahara; the Oriental region of Morocco; 
southern and northern Algeria; the Tamesna Plateau, Ténéré 
and Tin-Toumma Deserts in Niger; and most regions of Chad. 
Light to moderate rains also fell in southeastern Libya, central 
and western Algeria, and northern Mali. During the second 
dekad, the ITCZ shifted southward but remained from 50 to 
200 km north of its normal position, from eastern Mauritania to 
western Chad. Showers were recorded in various areas across 
Mauritania, northern Mali, southern Algeria, the Tamesna Plateau 
in Niger, and the southern parts of Kanem, Bahr-El-Gazel, 
Batha, and Wadi Fira regions in Chad. In the third dekad, the 
ITCZ moved close to its normal position, except in Mauritania 
where it was still located 250 to 300 km farther north. Heavy 
rains fell in southwestern Mauritania and northern Algeria, 
while light to moderate rains occurred in central Mauritania, 
northeastern Mali, northwestern Niger and the Wadi Fira and 
Ennedi regions of Chad. Green vegetation conditions persisted 
in the summer breeding areas from western Mauritania to 
Chad, although some areas—particularly the Aïr Mountains 
in Niger—were dry or drying. Vegetation remained green in 
irrigated areas of Adrar in Algeria.
CENTRAL REGION
In September, rainfall persisted in the summer breeding areas 
of the Region. The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone remained 
between 20 and 220 km north of its normal position in Sudan 
during the whole month. Light to moderate rains fell during 
the ﬁ rst dekad in North Darfur, North Kordofan, Khartoum, 
River Nile and the interior of Red Sea states of Sudan. Heavy 
rains fell in the Kassala state of Sudan, as well as the western 
lowlands of Eritrea. In the second and third dekads, heavy rains 
continued in Kassala, southern River Nile and western Red Sea 
states of Sudan, as well as the western lowlands of Eritrea. 
Sporadic showers continued to occur during the third dekad 
in all these same states of Sudan and western Eritrea, with 
a slight decrease in rainfall and spreading towards the north. 
Light rains fell along the Red Sea coast of Eritrea during the 
ﬁ rst two dekads. Light to moderate rains occurred during the 
whole month along the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia south of 
Jeddah, while heavy rains occurred along the coast of Yemen. 
On both sides of the Gulf of Aden, in Yemen and northern 
Somalia, light rains occurred during the ﬁ rst and third dekads 
while moderate rains were recorded during the second dekad. 
Light rains fell also in the interior of Yemen and Oman during 
the ﬁ rst dekad. Vegetation was green or greening in irrigated 
areas of Egypt, in most places in the interior of Sudan, such as 
along the Atbara and Nile Rivers, and on the western side of 
the Red Sea Hills while mainly dry vegetation was found along 
the Red Sea coasts of Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt. Vegetation 
was green between Jizan and Qunﬁ dah, slightly greening 
reaching Lith and still dry north of Lith, along the Red Sea 
coast of Saudi Arabia. In Oman’s interior, vegetation was dry.
EASTERN REGION
During September, monsoon rains decreased along the 
Indo-Pakistan border. In the ﬁ rst dekad, light to medium rains 
were recorded in Rajasthan in India and Cholistan, Nara, and 
Tharparkar Deserts in Pakistan, while heavy rainfall occurred 
in Gujarat in India. During the second dekad, moderate to 
heavy rainfall continued in Gujarat in India. In the third dekad, 
light rains persisted only in southern Rajasthan and Gujarat 
in India. Vegetation was green in Rajasthan and Gujarat in 
India as well as Pakistan’s Cholistan, Nara, and Tharparkar 
Deserts with some few places starting to dry. In Iran, vegetation 
was dry near the Jaz Murian Basin and in most places of 
South Khorosan, Hormozgan, and Fars regions while green 
vegetation was observed in some few places close to Shiraz 
and Bandar Abbas.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should connect to the Internet and 
backup the RAMSES database whenever data are added or 
changed; do not wait until the end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.
Regions
Western
•  Locust-affected countries in West and North-West Africa: 
Algeria, Chad, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, 
Senegal, Tunisia; during upsurges and plagues only: Benin, 
Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Gambia, 
Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierre 
Leone and Togo
Central

SMALL OUTBREAK IN MAURITANIA
 In August, a small locust outbreak developed in Mauritania, 
with hopper and breeding adult groups observed across the 
centre of the country, and where mature solitarious adults 
continued to be observed. Due to incomplete information, it 
remains uncertain whether similar outbreaks are occurring 
in other Sahelian countries. Isolated adults were seen in 
Chad. The signiﬁ cant rainfall across the Sahel during August 
continues to create favourable breeding conditions for dispersed 
locust populations. Numbers are expected to increase, with 
groups continuing to appear in Mauritania and potentially in 
Mali, Niger, Chad and eventually southern Algeria. Continued 
surveillance will be essential, and control measures will likely 
be necessary to contain potential outbreaks. In the Central 
Region, a few isolated and scattered adults were present in 
Sudan, where small-scale summer breeding may be occurring 
in the interior of the country. A few adults were also reported 
from Egypt. Breeding is expected to continue in Sudan and 
may begin in Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Yemen. In 
the Eastern Region, heavy monsoon rains persisted along 
the Indo–Pakistan border, but no locusts were found. Very 
small-scale breeding may still occur, though no signiﬁ cant 
developments are expected.

Rainfall decreased in all areas except in western Africa. 
Green vegetation remains in breeding areas of Mauritania 
and Western Sahara. Rainfall was sporadic along coastal 
areas of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
WESTERN REGION
During October, rainfall decreased across most Sahelian 
countries, except in the west. The Inter-Tropical Convergence 
Zone (ITCZ) shifted southward, approaching its normal position 
for this time of year. During the ﬁ rst dekad, moderate to heavy 
rainfall occurred in southern and western Mauritania and across 
Western Sahara. Light rains occurred in central and northern 
Mauritania, northeastern Mali, Tamesna and Aïr in Niger, the 
Hoggar Mountains in Algeria, and the Kanem region of Chad. 
In the second dekad, light to moderate rains were recorded in 
southern Mauritania and northern Algeria, while light rains fell in 
eastern Mauritania, central and western Algeria, northwestern 
Kidal in Mali, and northwestern Libya. During the third dekad, 
dry conditions prevailed across the region. Vegetation remained 
green in Mauritania and Western Sahara, providing favorable 
breeding conditions. In the Ennedi region, vegetation was 
drying out but remained green in Wadi Fira and some areas of 
Barh-El-Gazel in Chad. Green vegetation was also observed 
near irrigated areas in Adrar, Algeria. Vegetation conditions in 
Tunisia were predominantly dry.
CENTRAL REGION
In October, rainfall decreased across the region. The Inter-
Tropical Convergence Zone was 80 to 200 km north of its 
normal position in Sudan during the ﬁ rst dekad but shifted 
southward, approaching its usual position for the remainder 
of the month. Light to moderate rains fell during the ﬁ rst dekad 
in North Kordofan, Khartoum, Kassala and Red Sea states of 
Sudan. During the same period, showers occurred along the 
southern Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia and Eritrea, as well 
as in coastal areas of Yemen. Light to moderate rains also fell 
along the northwestern coast of Somalia and in the Plateau 
area. During the second dekad, drier conditions prevailed, 
except for some showers along the Red Sea coasts of Eritrea, 
Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia, as well as northwestern 
Somalia. During the third dekad, sporadic very light rains fell in 
Eritrea and Yemen. Vegetation remained green along the Nile 
and Atbara valleys, in the Bayuda Desert, and on the western 
side of the Red Sea Hills in Sudan, while most areas along the 
Red Sea coast of Egypt and Sudan were dry. Along the Red 
Sea coast and Hijaz Mountains of Saudi Arabia, vegetation was 
dry between Medina and Lith, with limited greening observed 
around Mecca, and then mostly green from Lith to Jizan in the 
south. Vegetation was dry in the interior and along the northern 
coast of Oman, as well as along the Gulf of Aden coast of Yemen 
while green was found in the interior Hadramaut. Greening 
was likely occurring in northwestern Somalia.
EASTERN REGION
During October, little rainfall occurred along the Indo-Pakistan 
border. In the ﬁ rst dekad, light to moderate rains fell in parts 
of Rajasthan and Gujarat in India, as well as in the Cholistan, 
Nara, and Tharparkar Deserts of Pakistan. During the second 
dekad, no rainfall was recorded except for light showers in 
Gujarat, India. In the third dekad, light rains persisted in eastern 
and southern Rajasthan and in Gujarat. Vegetation remained 
green in Rajasthan and Gujarat, although signs of drying were 
observed in some areas. In Pakistan, vegetation was mostly 
dry in the Cholistan, Nara, and Tharparkar Deserts, with only 
a few places with green vegetation. In Iran, vegetation was 
mainly dry near the Jaz Murian Basin, in most places of South 
Khorosan, Hormozgan, Bushehr and Fars regions while green 
vegetation was observed in a few places near Shiraz, Bandar 
Abbas, Birjand and Kahnuj.

A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.
Regions
Western
•  Locust-affected countries in West and North-West Africa: 
Algeria, Chad, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger,

OUTBREAK CONTINUES IN MAURITANIA
 In September, a locust outbreak continued to develop in 
Mauritania, where hopper groups ﬂ edge into immature adult 
groups across the central part of the country, and by the 
end of the month, new mature adult groups had started a 
second generation of breeding. A few isolated adults escaped 
to Senegal and bred locally. Scattered adults and hoppers 
were observed in eastern Niger, and isolated ones in several 
locations in Chad. A few isolated adults were found in Algeria. 
Ecological conditions remain favorable for breeding in many 
areas, although October and November are expected to be dry 
across most of the Sahel except its westernmost part. During 
the forecast period, locust numbers are expected to continue 
increasing, particularly in Mauritania, with new hopper groups 
appearing. Some adult groups may also appear in Mali, Niger, 
Chad, and eventually southern Algeria. Continued surveillance 
will be essential, and control measures will be necessary. In 
the Central Region, a few isolated and scattered adults were 
present in Sudan, where small-scale summer breeding may 
be occurring in the interior. Summer breeding is expected to 
conclude with a few groups possibly appearing in November. 
In the Eastern Region, monsoon rains declined along the 
Indo–Pakistan border, no locusts were found, and no signiﬁ cant 
developments are expected.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.

RAMSES data. Countries should connect to the Internet and 
backup the RAMSES database whenever data are added or 
changed; do not wait until the end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

Rainfall increased in December across all regions, with 
good rains occurring in Mauritania, Algeria, Libya, along 
the Red Sea coast and the interior of Saudi Arabia, and 
in Iran. Green vegetation persisted in breeding areas of 
Mauritania and Western Sahara and increased in Sudan,

WESTERN REGION
During December, rainfall occurred in Mauritania and in the 
spring breeding areas of Algeria, Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia. 
During the ﬁ rst dekad, light to heavy rains fell in western and 
central Mauritania, while light to moderate rains occurred in 
southeastern Algeria and southwestern Libya. Some light rains 
also fell in eastern Morocco, central Algeria and southeastern 
Tunisia. During the second dekad, moderate to heavy rains fell in 
southeastern, eastern and central Algeria, southern Tunisia and 
northwestern Libya. Light to moderate rains also fell in Western 
Sahara, Morocco, western Algeria, southwestern Libya, and 
northeastern Mali. During the third dekad, conditions returned 
to dry across the Region. Average temperatures dropped 
by 5° to 10°C between mid-November and mid-December, 
slowing locust population development and vegetation growth 
and decay. Vegetation was drying in northwestern Niger and 
southwestern Mauritania but was still green in northwestern 
Mauritania, northern Senegal, many sites in Western Sahara, the 
extreme south of Algeria and irrigated areas in central Algeria. 
In western Algeria and Morocco, most sites were drying or dry. 
Vegetation began greening in Tunisia.
CENTRAL REGION
In December, winter rains continued in the Red Sea area. 
During the ﬁ rst dekad, moderate to heavy rains fell in Saudi 
Arabia along the Red Sea coast between Jeddah and Al Wajh, 
as well as in the interior in the Hijaz Mountains and the spring 
breeding areas of Hail and Gassim. Light rains fell in southeast 
Egypt and along the northern Red Sea coast of Sudan. During 
the second dekad, light to moderate rains continued in the 
Gassim and Hail areas and extended to Riyad and Eastern 
Province of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and northern 
Oman. Light rains also fell near Qunﬁ dah and Jizan along the 
Red Sea in Saudi Arabia. During the third dekad, conditions 
remained dry across most desert locust winter breeding areas, 
but light rains were recorded near Hail and Gassim and in the 
Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. Vegetation was dry in the 
interior of southeastern Egypt but was green along the Wadi 
Diib, along the Red Sea near Halaib and in irrigated areas 
west of the Nile Valley, while greening was observed north of 
Abraq. Green and greening vegetation was also found along 
the Sudan Red Sea coast and in most places in the Red Sea 
Hills. Along the Saudi Arabian Red Sea coast, vegetation was 
mainly dry between Qunﬁ dah and Mecca but green south of 
Qunﬁ dah down to Jizan and green or greening north of Mecca 
up to Yenbo. On Yemen’s southern coast, vegetation was dry 
or drying near Mayfa’a and Bir Ali, as well as in most places 
around Aden and Zinjibar. In Oman, vegetation was dry except 
in a few places in Musandam Peninsula. 
EASTERN REGION
During December, heavy rains fell in Iran. After a particularly 
wet ﬁ rst dekad in northwest Iran, heavy rains fell along the 
southern coast from Bushehr to Sistan and Baluchistan during 
the second dekad. Light rains also fell in Balochistan, Pakistan. 
During the third dekad, sporadic light to moderate rains continued 
along the southern coast of Iran and light rains continued in 
southwest Pakistan. In India, vegetation was drying or dry in 
Rajasthan and Gujarat. In Iran, vegetation was dry in most 
places but began to appear green or greening near Bandar 
Abbas and Kahnuj.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should connect to the Internet and 
backup the RAMSES database whenever data are added or 
changed; do not wait until the end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.
eLocust3 digital tools
In addition to the original eLocust3 tablet, FAO has developed free 
tools for data collection in the ﬁ eld. Currently, the recommended 
one is eLocust3K, a smartphone app for survey and control 
data, based on KoboToolBox. 
The geo-referenced data collected by these tools feed into 
FAO’s global early warning system and are critical for real-time 
monitoring, near-instant analysis, and planning ﬁ eld operations 
in each country. 
[https://www.fao.org/locust-watch/activities/en]
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
FAO has developed pocket-sized SOPs for use on the ﬁ eld of 
Desert Locust biology, survey, and control, including instructions

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

Rainfall was limited in February across all three Regions, 
with only light rains reported in the spring breeding areas. 
Green vegetation increased in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, 
Saudi Arabia, and Iran but decreased in Mauritania, Western 
Sahara, Egypt, and Sudan.
WESTERN REGION
During February, light rains were concentrated on the northern 
part of the Region. During the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains fell in 
southern Tunisia, northeastern Algeria, northwestern Libya, 
along the Atlantic coast of Morocco and in the Canary Islands. 
The second dekad was dry in most Desert Locust habitats, 
but light rains occurred again in the Canary Islands. During 
the third dekad, light rains continued in Canary Islands and 
fell also in the Anti-Atlas, and in the Souss, Massa and Draa 
valleys of Morrocco as well as in western Algeria near Tindouf. 
On 24 February, easterly winds brought heat, dust, and locusts 
to the Canary Islands. Vegetation conditions were drying or 
already dry in southwestern and extreme northern Mauritania 
and in most of the southern part of Western Sahara, south of 
Bir Anzarane. Vegetation was mostly green along the Atlantic 
coast and north of Boucraa in Western Sahara, in most of 
southern Morocco and in northern Mauritania between Atar 
and Zouerate. Vegetation was green in most visited sites 
near Tindouf, in irrigated perimeters near Adrar and west of 
Beni Abbes in Algeria. Vegetation was green or greening in 
central Tunisia. 
CENTRAL REGION
In February, winter rains remained scarce along the Red Sea 
area and in most parts of the Region. During the ﬁ rst dekad, 
light rains fell very locally at a few sites along the Red Sea 
coast of Sudan and along the Gulf of Aden coasts of Yemen and 
Somalia. Light to moderate rains also occurred in the interior 
of Saudi Arabia. During the second dekad, light rains were 
recorded in northern Egypt. In the third dekad, very light rains 
fell along the Red Sea coast of Eritrea. Vegetation remained 
green in irrigated areas and in a few locations in southeastern 
Egypt. Vegetation began to dry out along the northern and 
central Red Sea coast of Sudan and along Wadi Diib but 
remained green in the southern part of the Red Sea coast. In 
Eritrea, a few green areas were present along the northern 
Red Sea coast. Along the central Red Sea coast of Saudi 
Arabia, between Lith and Masturah, vegetation was mostly 
dry while green vegetation was observed north of Masturah 
up to Duba along the northern Red Sea coast. In the interior 
of Saudi Arabia, vegetation was green or greening in some 
sites west of Gassim and south of Hail, although most areas 
remained dry. Vegetation was mostly dry in Oman. 
EASTERN REGION
During February, rains fell in spring breeding areas. In the ﬁ rst 
dekad, light to moderate rain fell in Iran along the southwestern 
and southeastern coasts, while light rains occurred in Balochistan, 
Pakistan. During the second dekad, light rains continued in 
Iran and increased slightly in Balochistan. In the third dekad, 
only very light rains were recorded in southwestern Iran. In 
India, vegetation was drying or dry in Rajasthan and Gujarat. 
In Iran, vegetation was mostly greening or green across the 
southern regions and in South Khorasan.

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should backup the RAMSES database 
and share it with FAO Desert Locust Information Service 
whenever data are added or changed; do not wait until the 
end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

The eLocust tools were developed by FAO since the 2000s to 
ease the survey and control data collection and transmission. 
The eLocust3 tablet is now being replaced by a new eLocust4 
tablet and antenna system. 
[https://www.fao.org/locust-watch/activities/dlis-home/elocust4/en]
In addition, FAO has developed a free tool for data collection 
in the ﬁ eld called eLocust3K, a smartphone app for survey 
and control data, based on KoboToolBox. 
[https://www.fao.org/locust-watch/activities/dlis-home/elocust3k/en]
The geo-referenced data collected by these tools feed into 
FAO’s global early warning system and are critical for real-time 
monitoring, near-instant analysis, and planning ﬁ eld operations 
in each country.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

Rainfall increased in March across all three Regions, with 
heavy rains reported in the spring breeding areas of Iran, 
Saudi Arabia, Oman and Algeria. Vegetation is green in 
Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia and likely green 
or greening in Iran and Pakistan.
WESTERN REGION
During March, spring rains increased across the northern part 
of the Region. During the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains fell in southern 
Tunisia, eastern Algeria, western Libya, the Oriental region and 
along the Atlantic coast of Morocco, as well as in the Canary 
Islands. During the second dekad, light to moderate rains 
occurred in northern and western Algeria, most of Morocco, 
southern parts of Western Sahara, the Canary Islands, the 
Tiris Zemmour region of Mauritania, northwestern Libya and 
southeastern Tunisia. During the third dekad, heavy rains fell 
in southwestern Algeria, while light to moderate rains continued 
in Morocco, the Canary Islands, western and central Algeria, 
and northwestern Libya. Light rains also affected southeastern 
Tunisia. Vegetation conditions were drying or already dry in 
most of southern Western Sahara, south of Boujdour, although 
localized green and moist areas were present near Aousserd 
and along the coast. Vegetation was green north of Guelta 
Zemmur and near Laayoune in Western Sahara, in most of 
southern Morocco, at all surveyed sites near Tindouf, and 
in irrigated perimeters near Adrar and west of Beni Abbes 
in Algeria. Vegetation was green or greening in central and 
southeastern Tunisia.
CENTRAL REGION
In March, rainfall increased substantially across the Arabian 
Peninsula. During the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains fell over Hail, 
Gassim, Riyadh and Makkah provinces in the interior of Saudi 
Arabia, while moderate to heavy rains affected the Eastern 
Province. During the second dekad, light to moderate rains 
occurred across all of Saudi Arabia and along the Red Sea 
coast of Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt as well as in the north of 
Egypt. During the third dekad, light to moderate rains fell over 
Saudi Arabia, Djibouti, northern Somalia and eastern Ethiopia, 
while heavy rains affected the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, 
Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, northern Oman, interior 
of Yemen, and northwestern Somalia. Vegetation was dry at 
most sites along the Red Sea coast of Sudan and along Wadi 
Diib, except for some green areas in the southern part of the 
Red Sea coast and in the interior north of Tomala. In Egypt, 
most surveyed sites were dry or drying, except irrigated areas 
near Tushka and some sites in the Sinai. Along the central 
Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia, between south of Jeddah and 
Yenbo, vegetation was mostly dry, while green vegetation was 
observed from Umm Lajj to Duba along the northern Red Sea 
coast. In the interior of Saudi Arabia, vegetation was green or 
greening around Gassim, in the southwest of Hail Province, 
and southeast of Al Dawadimi in Riyadh Province, but most 
other areas remained dry. Vegetation was mostly dry in Oman.
EASTERN REGION
During March, intense rainfall occurred in the spring breeding 
areas. During the ﬁ rst dekad, heavy rains fell in Fars, Bushehr 
and Kerman provinces of Iran, while light to moderate rains fell 
in all other provinces. During the second dekad, heavy rains 
affected the southwestern provinces of Iran and southwestern 
Pakistan, while light to moderate rains continued in southeastern 
Iran and fell also along the Indo-Pakistan border. During the 
third dekad, heavy rains persisted along the entire southern 
coast of Iran, and light to moderate rains fell in the interior of 
Iran and in southwestern Pakistan. Vegetation was likely green 
in most areas of southern Iran and may have begun to green 
in southwestern Pakistan. In India, vegetation was drying or

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.
Regions
Western
•  Locust-affected countries in West and North-West Africa: 
Algeria, Chad, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, 
Senegal, Tunisia; during upsurges and plagues only: Benin, 
Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Gambia, 
Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierre 
Leone and Togo

Regions, while heavy rains continued in the spring breeding 
areas of Saudi Arabia in the Central Region. Vegetation 
was green in Morocco, western Algeria, northern Oman

WESTERN REGION
During April, light to moderate rainfall occurred across the 
northern part of the Region. During the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains fell 
in the Oriental region and along the Atlantic coast of Morocco, 
in Western Sahara, as well as in the Canary Islands. Light rains 
also fell in northwestern Algeria and northern Libya. During the 
second and third dekads, light to moderate rainfall increased 
in northwestern Algeria and the Oriental region of Morocco, 
while light rains continued in northern Libya and, during the 
third dekad, spread to most of Algeria, northern Mali and 
southern Tunisia. Vegetation was drying or already dry in the 
Aïr Mountains of Niger and in most of southern Western Sahara, 
south of Boujdour; however, localized green and moist areas 
were present near Bir Gandouz and along the coast. Vegetation 
was green north of Guelta Zemmur and near Laayoune in 
Western Sahara, in most of southern Morocco, and at most 
surveyed sites in western Algeria from Tindouf to Aïn Sefra. 
In irrigated areas near Adrar in Algeria, vegetation remained 
green but was drying at many sites. Vegetation was green in 
central Tunisia but was drying in the southeast.

Peninsula. During the ﬁ rst dekad, light rains fell over Oman

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); 
signiﬁ cant threat to crops (intensive survey and control 
operations must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should backup the RAMSES database 
and share it with FAO Desert Locust Information Service 
whenever data are added or changed; do not wait until the 
end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

Other reporting terms
Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline
• A period characterised by breeding failure and/or suc cess ful 
control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.

Rainfall remained limited in May across the Western, Central 
and Eastern Regions, except south of the Atlas Mountains 
in Algeria and Morocco, in the Algeria-Libya border area, 
and in parts of Saudi Arabia, Somalia and Eritrea. Vegetation 
was green in Morocco, Algeria and southern Saudi Arabia,

WESTERN REGION
During May, rainfall occurred mainly in the northern part of 
the Region. Light rains fell during the ﬁ rst dekad south of the 
Atlas Mountains in Morocco and northwestern Algeria, as well 
as northern Libya, Tunisia, southwest Algeria and northern 
Mauritania. During the second dekad, light to moderate rains 
increased south of the Atlas Mountains in northeast Morocco 
and northwestern Algeria, while light rains persisted in northern 
Libya and Tunisia. During the third dekad, moderate to heavy 
rains fell in southeast Algeria and western Libya. Meanwhile, 
light rains fell in small parts of the summer breeding areas of 
northern Niger and northeastern Mali. Vegetation was drying or 
already dry in the Aïr Mountains of Niger and in most of Western 
Sahara. In Morocco, vegetation was green from Tan Tan to 
Guelmin, near Tata and Errachidia and in some areas of the 
Souss and Massa valleys between Tiznit and Agadir but began 
drying in many places south of the Atlas Mountains, particularly 
along the Draa and Taﬁ lalet valleys between Merzouga and 
Assa. In western Algeria, vegetation was green northwest of 
Aïn Sefra and at some sites near Tindouf, but dry elsewhere, 
while in the interior it remained green in most areas between 
Adrar and Timimoun. Vegetation was mostly drying or dry in 
central and southeastern Tunisia, except at a few sites.
CENTRAL REGION
During May, rainfall recessed across the region. Moderate to 
heavy rains fell during the ﬁ rst dekad in parts of the interior and 
Asir region of Saudi Arabia, the Red Sea coastal areas and 
western highlands of Yemen, as well as in Somalia, eastern 
Ethiopia and western Eritrea. Rainfall decreased markedly 
during the second dekad, with only light rains in Somalia and 
southeastern Sudan. During the third dekad, moderate to heavy 
rains occurred in southwestern Yemen, northern Somalia and 
eastern Ethiopia. Vegetation was mostly green in irrigated 
areas of Egypt near Hurghada, Aswan, Tushka, and along the 
New Valley from Sh. Oweinat to Farafra and Bahariya Oasis. 
Vegetation was mostly dry along the central Red Sea coast of

in parts of Qassim, Hail Province and southeast of Al Dawadimi 
in Riyadh Province, while most other areas remained dry. In

Dawasir. Vegetation was mostly dry in northern Oman, except

Amhara region near Bati and Kombolcha.
EASTERN REGION

No rain fell during any dekad in southern Iran or southwestern 
Pakistan. Light to moderate rain occured in northern Rajasthan 
in India and along the Indo-Pakistan border. Vegetation was 
likely drying in southern Iran and southwestern Pakistan. In 
India, vegetation was dry in Rajasthan and Gujarat, except in

Locust warning levels
A colour-coded scheme indicates the alert level, perceived 
risk, or threat of current Desert Locust infestations to crops, 
and appropriate response: 
• Green (calm) – calm situation (low alert); no threat to crops 
(maintain regular monitoring)
• Yellow (caution) – cautious situation (moderate alert); 
potential threat to crops (increased vigilance, control may 
be needed)
• Orange (threat) – serious situation (high alert); threat to 
crops (survey and control must be undertaken)
• Red (danger) – dangerous situation (very high alert); signiﬁ cant 
threat to crops (intensive survey and control operations 
must be conducted)
The scheme is applied to the Locust Watch web page and the 
monthly bulletins and updates.
Locust reporting
RAMSES data. Countries should backup the RAMSES database 
and share it with FAO Desert Locust Information Service 
whenever data are added or changed; do not wait until the 
end of the month.
Bulletins. Affected countries are encouraged to prepare decadal, 
fortnightly, or monthly bulletins that summarize and analyze 
the situation, and share them with other countries.
Reporting. All information should be sent by e-mail to the 
FAO Desert Locust Information Service (eclo@fao.org and 
faodlislocust@gmail.com). Reports received by the ﬁ rst day 
of the new month will be included in the FAO Desert Locust 
Bulletin; otherwise, they will not appear until the following 
month. Reports should be sent even if no locusts were found 
or if no surveys were conducted.

Breeding
•  The process of reproduction from copulation to ﬂ edg ing.
Recession
•  Period without widespread and heavy infestations by swarms.
Remission
•  Period of deep recession marked by the complete absence 
of gregarious populations.
Outbreak
• A marked increase in locust numbers due to con cen tra tion, 
multiplication and gregarisation which, unless checked, can 
lead to the formation of hopper bands and swarms.
Upsurge
•  A period following a recession marked initially by a very large 
increase in locust numbers and con tem po ra ne ous outbreaks 
followed by the production of two or more successive seasons 
of transient-to- gre gar i ous breeding in complimentary seasonal 
breed ing areas in the same or neighbouring Desert Lo cust 
regions.
Plague
•  A period of one or more years of widespread and heavy 
infestations, the majority of which occur as bands or swarms. 
A major plague exists when two or more regions are affected 
simultaneously.
Decline

control leading to the dissociation of swarm ing populations 
and the onset of recessions; can be regional or major.
